newsitem.title: USA: Defense logs partial sucesss in Oklahoma bomb trial.
newsitem.headline: Defense logs partial sucesss in Oklahoma bomb trial.

text.p: The defence in the Oklahoma City bombing trial succeeded in attacking the character of a star government witness -- but could not detract from the power of his testimony against Timothy McVeigh, legal experts say.

Michael Fortier on Monday gave the most damning evidence so far against his former Army buddy McVeigh, who is accused of blowing up the Oklahoma City federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people in the worst attack against civilians in U.S. history.
Fortier, 28, said McVeigh had told him in 1994 he was planning the attack in an attempt to start a "general uprising" against the U.S. government.
In a cross-examination dripping with sarcasm on Tuesday, chief defence attorney Stephen Jones focused on trying to undermine Fortier's credibility.
Fortier, in a plea bargain with prosecutors, has pleaded guilty to four felony counts in return for testifying that he knew about plans for the bombing but did nothing to stop it.
Jones emphasised that Fortier sold and used drugs, had repeatedly lied to authorities and had committed a number of crimes apart from the ones he had been charged with.
Jones also showed that Fortier, who is in jail awaiting sentencing, had an interest in pleasing the prosecution to win a lighter punishment than the 23-year jail term he could be sentenced to.
But while Fortier conceded many of the character issues, he stuck to his story about McVeigh's alleged statements to him.

"I don't think they poked many holes in the core of his testimony. What they did was try to poke holes in him as a person who would give honest testimony. Instead of trying to attack the message, you try to kill the messenger," said Andrew Cohen, a Denver lawyer and legal analyst for CBS News.

Jones had made as much as he could of Fortier's weaknesses, Cohen said. But Cohen said he still believed Fortier was an effective government witness. "He ties a lot of things together, closes the circle about the plot," he said.
McVeigh, a decorated Gulf War veteran, has pleaded not guilty to charges of murder and conspiracy. He could face the death penalty if convicted.

Jones forced Fortier to concede he had lied several times on official gun sales records when he falsely said he was not a marijuana user and yet signed the forms as being true. "I stand corrected. I committed this crime also," Fortier said.
Jones pointed out that Fortier's image had been transformed from his unkempt look when he lived in Arizona to his businesslike appearance in court where he wore a suit and had his hair cut short.

Fortier also conceded he had spent up to 175 hours with prosecutors or FBI agents since his arrest. He said prosecutors had put him through a mock cross-examination before the trial but denied they had coached him on what to say.
Denver defence attorney David Japha said Jones had done a very good cross-examination but had been unable to get Fortier to admit that anything he said on the witness stand was a lie.

Japha said it was a brilliant move by the prosecution to immediately follow Fortier's appearance with testimony from an FBI photographer who said investigators asked her to photograph a key found in an alley near the federal building three days after the bombing. Prosecutors say it was the key to the Ryder rental truck that McVeigh allegedly used in the bombing.
The testimony about the key tied in neatly with Fortier's allegation that McVeigh told him months before the bombing that he planned to park his getaway car in the alley.

A lock expert testified later on Tuesday that the key fitted a type of lock used on a 1993 Ford F700 truck, the model that the government says McVeigh rented. The expert, Charles Edwards, faces more tough questions from the defence when court resumes on Wednesday.
